newsitem.title: USA: OMB chief makes no promises on DC's fed payment.
newsitem.headline: OMB chief makes no promises on DC's fed payment.

text.p: The Office of Management and Budget's chief said Thursday that the Clinton Administration will consider requests for a continued annual federal payment to the beleaguered District of Columbia, but made no promises on the issue.

"We understand that the committee may have additional ideas that it would like to put forward, and we would be happy to talk to the committee about those," Franklin Raines said at a congressional hearing on President Clinton's new revitalization proposal for the District.

Raines was responding to a question on the issue by Rep. Thomas Davis, R-Va., chairman of the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee's subpanel on D.C, which conducted the hearing. Davis had asked whether the administration would remain "flexible" on the federal payment or its thinking "fixed" on the subject.
The District currently gets a $660 million federal payment in lieu of taxes for the federal government's use of District properties.

But in a $3.9 billion, five-year revitalization plan for the Nation's Capital announced January 14, the White House proposed wiping out the annual payment in return for a major federal aid package for the city.

In other comments, Raines offered additional details on a White House's plan to establish an economic development corporation (EDC) for the city that would be funded in part with federal funds, with an increasing local and private sector match.

Raines said the corporation's funding would not be focused on a particular area in the city. Instead, it would be available to projects in the city's central business district and surrounding low income communities, he said.
"It is not our current thinking that (the corporation) would be active in the higher income areas where there is a considerable amount of economic activity," he said.
Raines said the corporation would be made up "primarily of private-sector individuals appointed by some combination of the federal and local governments."
"It is our desire to attract private capital to the corporation to supplement the funds made available by the federal government," Raines said.
He said the new authority could give business tax breaks and have control over surplus District land.

"We think it would be very beneficial for the corporation to have access to land," Raines said. "It would be our hope to make available lands that they could declare a surplus ... available for economic development."
The corporation could oversee activities ranging from major development projects to job training and job creation, Raines said.
But he said there would be more reliance on tax systems and incentives than direct fedeal appropriations.

Panel chairman Davis said the federal and District governments are at a "crossroads" on helping the city. "Rarely do we face a situation where all the major political winds are aligned in one direction," he said.
President Clinton and congressional leaders recently named overhaul of D.C. finances as one of their top five joint projects for the near future.
Davis said, "We must take advantage of this positive environment.".
Raines said the White House's goal is for Congress to clear a D.C. financial overhaul bill this spring.
